Communication sent to the UN Working Group on Business & Human Rights, the UN Special Rapporteur on Poverty, the UN Special Rapporteur on the Right to Health, and the UN Special Rapporteur on Freedom of Association

We write to submit information regarding systematic human rights violations committed by the world’s largest corporations, Amazon and Walmart, against their workforces. These companies have normalized abusive behavior in their warehouses and stores, adopting a range of labor practices intended to maximize profits at the cost of worker health and safety. This includes deploying surveillance technology that generates high rates of injury, stifling unions, and paying grossly inadequate wages that force employees to work multiple jobs or rely on public assistance. These companies also benefit from and perpetuate racial and class inequalities in the United States: research confirms that the labor violations and economic harms generated by these companies are particularly pronounced for Black Americans and women. These abuses not only demonstrate the immediacy of human rights concerns across Amazon’s and Walmart’s operations, but are illustrative of the companies’ contribution to poverty and deepening economic inequalities.

As the two largest private employers both in the United States 1 and across the globe, 2 these businesses exercise outsized influence on the enjoyment of human rights. While the labor abuses documented in this communication are occurring across the U.S., Amazon’s dehumanizing labor practices are being exported to its warehouses across the globe, 3 while Walmart’s 4 and Amazon’s 5 global supply chains are rife with allegations of serious human rights abuses, including forced labor, human trafficking, and exploitation.

We appreciate that the UN Special Rapporteur on Poverty Olivier De Schutter raised these concerns in 2023, commenting that “I am extremely disturbed that workers in some of the world's most profitable companies – in one of the richest countries on earth – are struggling to afford to eat or pay their rent. Multi-billion dollar companies should be setting the standard for working conditions and wages, not

violating the human rights of their workers by failing to pay them a decent wage.” 6 The persistence and even deepening of these labor abuses merits continued attention.

We respectfully request that the special mandates send a communication to Amazon and Walmart to inquire about their plans to mitigate these pervasive violations. In particular, we request that the companies adopt the labor policies listed on pages 8-9 in order to protect worker health and safety, the practices listed on pages 13-14 in order to minimize their adverse impacts on poverty and inequality, and the approach to unions listed on pages 16-17 to ensure they are respecting freedom of association. We also respectfully request that the special mandates send a communication to the U.S. government, which has an obligation to ensure that companies headquartered and operating in its territory are not committing widespread human rights abuses. In particular, we request that the U.S. government pursue policies laid out on pages 9-10, 14-15, and 17.

I. AMAZON AND WALMART OPERATE DANGEROUS WORK ENVIRONMENTS, EXACERBATED

BY SURVEILLANCE TECHNOLOGY

Amazon and Walmart are imposing labor policies that sacrifice the wellbeing of workers in a drive for profit maximization. This includes deploying new, dystopian methods to exploit and punish employees in a bid to speed up production.

The rise in surveillance technology has emerged as one particularly oppressive tactic that generates concerning health and safety records at both companies. According to documents filed with the National Labor Relations Board (NLRB), Amazon’s “time off task” (TOT) policy automatically penalizes workers for pausing or moving at slower rates, pressuring employees to work at an unsafe pace. 7 Managers closely track an employee’s speed of movement, and the looming threat of sanctions – including termination – place painful physical and mental demands on employees who fear the repercussions should they fail to meet undisclosed productivity goals. 8 Security cameras are trained on Amazon’s warehouse floors so that managers can monitor whether a worker is away from their station for too long, while employee badges enable managers to track where their workers’ location and length of any rest breaks. 9 As warehouse worker [Amazon Worker] describes,

“They monitor us with cameras. They have cameras throughout their whole building. They also have process assistants who walk around just to see if you're on your phone so they can write you up…They just try to find things that basically write you up for...three write ups leads to disciplinary action….It's not a good feeling at all because it's like we're in prison. Like, y'all fitting to monitor us 24/7, as if we're like trying to do something wrong.” 10

These oppressive tactics have not gone unnoticed. National Labor Relations Board General Counsel Jennifer Abruzzo observed in a 2022 memo that the “omnipresent surveillance and other algorithmic management tools” are used for “disciplining employees who fall short of quotas, penalizing employees for taking leave, and providing individualized directives throughout the workday.” 11 This level of scrutiny creates physical and mental stress that discourage workers from using the bathroom, drinking water, or simply resting from such physically demanding work.

While Amazon pioneered the practice in its warehouses, 12 Walmart followed suit and is similarly accelerating technology use to monitor workers. A September 2024 research report explains, “[t]he introduction of new monitoring technologies results in many Walmart warehouse workers feeling constantly under watch and compelled to work at unsustainable rates.” 13 In a survey of 444 workers

across 35 states, the majority of workers reported that the level of monitoring or surveillance surpassed what they experienced in other workplaces, 14 and 67% reported that their speed of work was always or almost always monitored by the company. 15 An employee explains that “there is a camera that constantly watches everything anybody does… [we are] definitely under surveillance and feel like I'm being watched all the time…they can see everything you do with the handheld. They know what block you’re on [during deliveries]…and [you are] discouraged from talking [with coworkers]…makes it for a very drab and prison-like work environment.” 16 Scholars developed the phrase “Walmartism” to capture aggressive corporate surveillance, defining it as authority that is flexed through “a penetrative system of observation, measurement, and feedback that constrains both workers and managers—a system assembled from technological innovations unavailable to Walmart’s nineteenth-century counterparts.” 17 This surveillance technology is being deployed across storefronts and shipment centers.

1. Physical Impacts of Surveillance

Research, worker surveys, and government reprimand illustrate that the companies’ surveillance and discipline regime’s unrelenting pressure to move faster and faster in an inherently dangerous work environment has led to a spike in serious injuries throughout the companies’ warehouses and stores. For example:

• Amazon o Data from the U.S. government’s Occupational Safety and Health Organization (OSHA) confirms that Amazon’s overall injury rate climbed 20% between 2020 and 2021, and that the company was responsible for an alarming 49% of warehouse injuries in the U.S. in 2021 (despite employing only 33% of warehouse workers). 18 The company’s injury rate remains higher than the warehousing industry average of 5.5 per 100 full-time workers in 2022. 19 As Amazon employee [Amazon worker] explains, these are avoidable injuries with minimal company oversight: “I don't feel like it's accidental because so many people are getting hurt, injured within that same department.” 20 o The Strategic Organizing Center (SOC) references the Amazon “injury machine” as one beset by a culture of intimidation and reprimand. 21 This included workers being forced to urinate into bottles to avoid going to the bathroom and risk missing their productivity goals. 22 o The company’s injury rate dropped in 2020, when Amazon briefly paused the TOT mandates due to COVID restrictions; this illustrates the link between the grueling pace that surveillance technology incites and high injury rates. 23 o As a warehouse worker from North Carolina related in an interview, “Working at Amazon is, I don’t know if you ever watched … Squid Game. … It is a degrading job [with] this constant surveillance. You’re standing constantly. A lot of workers … have been standing on those hard concrete floors for so long, we have lower-back issues. We have other issues that are going on physically with our bodies. If you take our facility alone, since the facility opened, every three days, first responders are called to that facility. And when I say that it’s like [Squid Game], you see co-workers, you see friends, some workers have relatives, you see relatives who pass out, who are taken out of their facility on the stretcher.” 24 o An Amazon employee working out of a North Carolina warehouse commented that after she hurt her shoulder and neck at work, “they send you to their doctors [stationed within the facility] who basically just tell you to go back out on the floor….They really have minimal knowledge of healthcare.” 25 

o An Amazon employee also commented, “there's so many injuries, I don't even know 
where to start. It's almost like you go to Amazon, you leave out of the place with 
PTSD, with seeing people that you work with, you eat lunch with…. This is how you treat 
bodies. They’re just replaceable.” 26 
o Another former Amazon employee commented that “I left Amazon because my body 
couldn’t handle it anymore. If you don’t move the box, the next person will move the box. 
... They’re ready to jump onto the next person. When someone gets that thought into your 
head that you’re so easily replaceable, you’re more willing to ignore your injuries. ... One 
of my biggest concerns was what was I going to injure today.” 27 
• Walmart o Walmart carries the dubious distinction of ranking as the U.S. company with the second highest rate of severe workplace injuries between 2015 and 2022. 28 o OSHA has repeatedly fined Walmart for worker health and safety violations across its warehouses and stores. 29 o 38% of Walmart workers surveyed who had been at the company for five years or more report having been injured on the job. 30 o Employees are effectively discouraged from seeking medical care when they do endure injuries or fall ill. This is due to the company’s notoriously harsh “point system” that disciplines and potentially terminates employees for violations such as missing work, which includes absences to seek medical care for injuries suffered in Walmart warehouses. 31 o A survey of over 1,000 workers revealed that Walmart routinely refused to accept doctor’s notes to excuse an absence, and punished workers for medical absences. 32 ▪ As one former Walmart worker recounts, “My appendix ruptured while at work and because I already had eight points, I could not leave work to go to the emergency room (ER) without pointing out and losing my job. I should have been able to leave to go to the ER and not worry about losing my job. I had even said to managemen
